clue.text: Players count bung in shed

definitions.meaning: an old sense: to add up or compute figures
as a snake sheds or sloughs its skin

explanation.surface: Actors totting up the takings while chucking something into a garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: Four separate meanings strung together; 'bung' is British slang for throw, and the adding-up sense of 'count' is old-fashioned but in Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: The one short word covers a company of actors, reckoning figures, throwing, and discarding a skin.

clue.text: Doctor Livingstone's first cousin taking on Conservative for the final time

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered into a new order
'first' keeps only the first letter of 'Livingstone'

parts.note: opening letter of the explorer's name
the word on, taken as written

explanation.surface: A plea, perhaps, to Dr Livingstone's relative to take on the Tories one last time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor Livingstone' reads as the famous explorer's title, but 'Doctor' is the anagram signal and only his first letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A conclusion is the ending, the last occasion something happens, as in the phrase 'in conclusion'.

clue.text: Dumb way to take heroin … bare dumb

indicators.note: to bare something is to strip it, here stripping away its outer letters
one thing takes another in when it holds it inside itself

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
the second dumb with its first and last letters stripped off

explanation.surface: A dazed drug user rendered speechless, said with a trailing pause.
explanation.walkthrough: SH(T) is ST holding H. Shtum, from Yiddish, is British slang for silent, as in 'keep shtum'.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping shtum means saying nothing, so it is a synonym for dumb in the sense of silent.

clue.text: Tell star playing in clubs about refreshing keys

indicators.note: the rearranged letters sit inside the two single letters that follow
letters that are playing are moving about freely, so they are rearranged

parts.note: C is the card-suit abbreviation for clubs
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Tell a celebrity performing at nightclubs about some refreshing keys, perhaps on a piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refreshing keys' suggests piano music, but it is a computer key combination pressed together to reset or refresh things.
explanation.definitionFit: Control, Alt and Escape are three keyboard keys pressed together as a shortcut to restart or recover a stuck screen.

clue.text: Already coming back to take list (it's useful for shopping)

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it inside
something coming back travels the other way, so the word is read from right to left

parts.note: yet can mean already, as in 'has he come yet?'
a roll is a list of names, as in roll call

explanation.surface: Someone already heading back to pick up their shopping list.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits in the closing bracket, posing as an aside about the list.
explanation.definitionFit: A trolley is the wheeled basket pushed around a supermarket, so it is genuinely useful for shopping.

clue.text: Sir Christopher's part of the hospital is on the quiet side

parts.note: Sir Christopher Lee, the actor famous for Dracula
a hospital is divided into wards

explanation.surface: A knight's hospital ward is in the calmer wing of the building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sir Christopher' might suggest Wren, but it is the actor Lee.
explanation.definitionFit: Leeward is the side sheltered from the wind, hence calmer and quieter than the windward side.

clue.text: Kids' hits on the radio

indicators.note: radio is heard rather than seen, so the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: to lam is to thrash or hit hard

explanation.surface: Children's songs getting airplay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kids' hits' reads as chart songs for children; 'Kids' is the definition, in the sense of young animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambs, like kids, are young farm animals, and both are used fondly for children.

clue.text: Getting rid of former Russian president's no good for Middle Eastern Gulf

indicators.note: one thing given for another takes its place in the word

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
NG is the abbreviation for no good
G is an abbreviation for gulf on maps

explanation.surface: Removing an ex-Kremlin leader is no good for the Gulf states.
explanation.walkthrough: NG replaces the T in PUTIN, giving PUNGIN, then G is added. 'Middle Eastern Gulf' looks like geography but splits into a letter selection and an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To expunge is to erase or remove completely, so expunging means removing something entirely.

clue.text: Suggests lines to the audience

indicators.note: an audience listens, so the word is taken by its sound

explanation.surface: A prompter feeding an actor's lines to the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines' and 'audience' paint a theatre, but lines here are queues of people.
explanation.definitionFit: To cue someone is to prompt or hint at what they should do, so cues means suggests.

clue.text: Upset, the first lady is on a horse ride half-cut

indicators.note: cutting something in half loses one of its halves

parts.note: gee-gee is a child's word for a horse
the first half of the word
Eve, the first woman in Genesis

explanation.surface: The president's wife is upset after a drunken horse ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for tipsy, but here it halves a word. 'First lady' suggests a president's wife but means Eve.
explanation.definitionFit: To aggrieve is to distress or wrong someone, so it is a verb meaning to upset.

clue.text: Arranged to spring a trap

indicators.note: to spring a prisoner is to free them, so the following letter escapes from the word

parts.note: the letter that is let out

explanation.surface: Someone set things up to spring a trap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring a trap' looks like one idiom; 'spring a' frees the A from NEAT, and 'trap' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To net something is to catch it, as a fisherman does, so it is a verb synonym for trap.

clue.text: Feel up when nothing goes wrong

indicators.note: something that goes wrong is thrown into disorder, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, also part of the signal

explanation.surface: Someone's dejection after a day where nothing went right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Goes' does double duty, as fodder and inside the signal 'goes wrong'. 'Feel up' reads as cheer up but means a grope.
explanation.definitionFit: To goose someone is slang for poking or groping them from behind, much like to feel someone up.

clue.text: Politician takes a beat, cutting out dead wood

indicators.note: a word that takes another holds it within itself
cutting something out removes it from the word

parts.note: to have led a race is to have been ahead, beating the rest
D is the abbreviation for dead

explanation.surface: A politician on the beat, pruning dead wood from the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dead wood' is a stock phrase, but 'dead' belongs to the deletion and 'wood' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Maple is a hardwood tree whose timber is used for furniture and floors, an example of wood.

clue.text: Primate holding bird in both hands

indicators.note: the outer letters hold the bird between them

parts.note: L and R, left and right

explanation.surface: A monkey cradling a bird in its two hands.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemurs are tree-dwelling primates native to Madagascar.

clue.text: Feel sick about one child's secret love affairs

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to ail is to be unwell

explanation.surface: Feeling queasy on discovering one's child is having secret affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A liaison is a clandestine romantic or sexual relationship, so the plural matches secret love affairs.

clue.text: Nasty racist does solitary

definitions.note: solitary as an adjective, 'ostracised' as a participle used adjectivally

indicators.note: something nasty is twisted and spoilt, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: An unpleasant bigot ends up in solitary confinement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does solitary' reads as serving time in isolation; 'does' is fodder and 'solitary' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ostracised is shut out by everyone, so left alone and isolated.

clue.text: Big setback being a hundred and one before your first club!

indicators.note: something set back is pushed the opposite way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: OS is outsize, a clothing label for big

indicators.note: 'first' keeps only the first letter of 'your'

explanation.surface: A centenarian's milestone birthday being celebrated before joining a club.
explanation.walkthrough: ET as 'being' is the film's extra-terrestrial; some solvers read it as Latin et instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A society is an organised association of members with a shared interest, the same thing as a club.

clue.text: Up and down, like second column?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: marked by ups and downs, as in a varied career
second meaning: the grid's second column alternates black and white squares

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition refers to this very grid: its second column runs light, dark, light, dark like a chessboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A career with mixed fortunes is called chequered, and a pattern of alternating squares is chequered too.

clue.text: Revolutionary had a slip taking out power plants

indicators.note: a revolution turns everything over, so the letters are rearranged
taking out a letter removes it from the fodder

parts.note: P is the symbol for power

explanation.surface: A rebel slipped up while removing a power station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Power plants' reads as generating stations; 'power' belongs to the deletion and 'plants' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dahlias are flowering garden plants with showy blooms, named after the botanist Dahl.

clue.text: Ambassador on a date? What about back problem?

parts.note: D is an abbreviation for date

indicators.note: going back means the two preceding words run in the opposite direction

parts.note: eh? is a way of saying what?

explanation.surface: A diplomat out on a date wonders about his back trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back problem' looks like one unit; 'back' reverses the previous pair and 'problem' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A headache is a figurative nuisance or worry, so it is a synonym for problem.

clue.text: Roast is missing hot stuff

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so that letter drops out

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A roast lacks anything spicy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot stuff' reads as a phrase, but 'stuff' is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff yourself is to eat far too much, which is what overeating means.

clue.text: Books mid-October to chase bull in Spanish city

indicators.note: what chases comes after, so these pieces follow the next one

parts.note: New Testament, a collection of books

indicators.note: mid- asks for the central letter of the month named

parts.note: the central letter of the seven

explanation.surface: Reading in mid-October before chasing a bull through a Spanish city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spanish city' suggests Pamplona's bull run, but 'Spanish' belongs to the bull and the city is Canadian.
explanation.definitionFit: Toronto is the largest city in Canada, the capital of Ontario.

clue.text: Soldiers and last bit of egg sent back on tea tray

parts.note: char is British slang for tea

indicators.note: sent back means returned in the other direction, so the pair is read backwards
the final letter of the next word is the one kept

explanation.surface: Toast soldiers and the end of a boiled egg sent back on a breakfast tray.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'soldiers' are strips of toast for dipping in a boiled egg, a strong decoy here.
explanation.definitionFit: A charger is a large flat serving dish or platter, close enough to a tray.

clue.text: Reading unknown, almost one Celsius above and one Celsius below frozen

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a single C for Celsius, placed at the top of this down entry
reading is one of the three Rs
I for one and C for Celsius, at the bottom

explanation.surface: A thermometer reading near zero, a degree above or below freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: The temperature talk hides the placing: in a down entry 'above' means at the top and 'below' at the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryonic describes deep-freezing bodies for preservation, so it means kept frozen.

clue.text: Bake Off presenter has posh trainee replacing a line. Shade!

indicators.note: replacing means swapping one thing in where another was

parts.note: Mary Berry, long-time judge and face of the TV baking show
A plus RY, railway, a line

explanation.surface: A TV baking presenter with a well-spoken apprentice taking a dig at someone.
explanation.walkthrough: UL replaces ARY in the first name. 'Shade!' looks like slang for an insult but is the definition, a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Mulberry is a dark purplish-red colour, named after the fruit, so it is a shade.

clue.text: Calling for bill in this manner suggests one's unwell — aww!

parts.words: Calling for bill in this manner suggests one's unwell
parts.note: surface reading: a cheeky way of asking for the bill hints you feel poorly

parts.words: Calling for bill in this manner
parts.note: setter's reading: take the answer as an instruction, the letter B taken away, and apply it to the word bill, leaving a word meaning unwell

explanation.surface: Asking for the bill in a funny way makes it sound like you are poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as B-LESS: bill with B removed leaves ILL, which is why it suggests being unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'bless!' is a fond exclamation at something sweet or pitiable, just like 'aww!'.

clue.text: Cobbled together a house in Washington

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the city abbreviation

parts.note: HO is an abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: A house in the US capital thrown together hastily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A house in Washington' tempts you toward the White House.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad hoc means improvised for a particular need rather than planned, so hastily cobbled together.

clue.text: Fellow has to back Student Raffles, for instance

indicators.note: one word that has another holds it inside
back means the short word is turned the other way round

explanation.surface: A man must support Raffles, the gentleman-thief student.
explanation.walkthrough: Raffles suggests the fictional cracksman, but here it is the famous colonial hotel in Singapore.
explanation.definitionFit: The Raffles in Singapore is a celebrated luxury hotel, so it is an example of one.

clue.text: Film about boring mathematical equation

indicators.note: boring into something means going inside it

parts.note: a sum, loosely a mathematical calculation

explanation.surface: A dull movie about a maths formula.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' suggests a movie, but it is the layer of dirt on a liquid's surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Scum is a thin layer of froth or dirt floating on a liquid, a film in that sense.

clue.text: Bad luck dogs the finale

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so the last letter is taken

explanation.surface: Misfortune follows a play to its final act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dogs' reads as a verb, misfortune hounding someone, but it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A curse is an evil spell or persistent misfortune, so bad luck.

clue.text: Partial fraction (in theory)?

indicators.note: partial means only part of the following words is used

parts.note: spans the end of fraction, all of in and the start of theory

explanation.surface: A maths term for a part of a fraction, theoretically speaking.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the hiding place and the definition: the answer is a fraction, and only part of a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A ninth is a fraction, one of nine equal parts, so it is partial in the sense of being a part.

clue.text: Sit back, it is a contraction!

indicators.note: back means the word runs in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: A midwife telling a woman in labour to sit back during a contraction.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Tis is the poetic shortening of the two words, so it is a contraction for them.

clue.text: Power wielded by king amidst reshuffle? That hurts

indicators.note: a reshuffle reorders things, so these letters change places

explanation.surface: A monarch's authority exercised during a cabinet reshuffle that causes pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reshuffle' suggests politics, but here it rearranges the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: King Midas of myth could turn whatever he touched to gold, a power wielded by a king.

clue.text: Tramp's fuzz

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to walk heavily and wearily
second meaning: British slang for the police

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp's fuzz' suggests a vagrant's stubble; 's means is, and both words are definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To plod is to trudge slowly, and 'the plod' is slang for the police, like 'the fuzz'.
